Denver Healing Could Move a Nun Jailed by Communists Toward Sainthood The postulator of Blessed Zdenka Schelingová’s cause has delivered the dossier on an alleged Denver healing to the archbishop of Bratislava, advancing her path toward canonization. An official portrait depicts Blessed Zdenka Schelingová, beatified in 2003 (photo: Archive of the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross ) Bohumil Petrík/EWTN News English Nation August 9, 2026 Blessed Zdenka Schelingová, a Slovak religious member of the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross (SCSC), may be one step closer to sainthood. The postulator of her cause, Father Lucián Bogucki of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual, handed the positio super miro to Archbishop Stanislav Zvolenský of Bratislava, last month. The document, whose Latin title refers to a purported miracle, describes an alleged healing said to have occurred through her intercession in Denver. “The very fact that the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints is dealing with the extraordinary healing through the intercession of Blessed Zdenka Schelingová is a gift from God and a great encouragement,” Archbishop Zvolenský told EWTN News. The date for the meeting of the commission of cardinals that will discuss the document and the reported miracle is not yet known but may come within a few months. The final decision on canonization rests with the Pope. The cause is an opportunity to enter “spiritual communion with those whom the Church presents to us as saints and blessed, so that we can also turn to them with a request for their intercession,” the archbishop said. Archbishop Zvolenský encouraged the faithful to “admire God’s goodness, as he always gives us extraordinary signs of his love.” A Martyr Under Communism Born Cecília Schelingová on Christmas Eve 110 years ago in the village of Krivá, in modern-day Slovakia, the future sister joined the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross and worked as a nurse and later in a hospital laboratory. She helped a Catholic priest escape from a hospital and attempted to do so again; the second time, it was a trap, and she was arrested. She was tortured, accused of treason by the recently established communist regime, and imprisoned in various jails across then-Czechoslovakia. Blessed Zdenka Schelingová appears in a 1952 Czechoslovak State Security photograph taken after her arrest in Bratislava. | Credit: Archive of the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross (SCSC) Sister Zdenka was released in April 1955 and died on July 31, 1955, from the effects of torture and her ruined health. She was exonerated of all charges against her in 1970 and was beatified in 2003 by Pope John Paul II. Respect and admiration for Sister Zdenka “is growing,” as “we have seen this now during various events on her liturgical feast,” which falls on July 30, said Sister Mária Terézia Dobrovičová, provincial superior of the Slovak province of the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross. The congregation was founded 170 years ago in Switzerland, and soon afterward the sisters were invited to what is now Slovakia, she explained. Bishop Tomáš Galis of the Diocese of Žilina celebrated Mass on the feast day, quoting Sister Zdenka: “Forgiveness is the greatest thing in life.” The Confederation of Political Prisoners of Slovakia also organized a conference on the religious sisters who lived in secret under the communist regime in Czechoslovakia. Pilgrims are visiting sites associated with her, including her native village of Krivá; Podunajské Biskupice, where her remains rest; and Trnava, the seat of the congregation in Slovakia. Sister Mária Terézia said the sisters “receive various requests from people to pray for the intercession” of Sister Zdenka, “but we also have various testimonies about how prayers for her intercession have been heard.” This is encouraging, “and we are happy about it,” she stressed. Cecília Schelingová, the future Blessed Zdenka, is pictured as a 15-year-old, around the time she entered religious life. | Credit: Archive of the Sisters of Mercy of the Holy Cross (SCSC) The official website dedicated to Sister Zdenka’s memory, Zdenka.sk , shares several testimonies from people whose prayers were answered after they prayed to her. It does not, however, include the case contained in the positio super miro. The Denver Healing A man in Denver was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer and sent home. His wife knew someone who was a distant relative of Sister Zdenka and, together with her colleagues, reportedly began to pray for him. The man had his tubes removed and was ready to die, yet his appetite returned and he regained his strength. He later suffered an embolism and died, according to one Slovak daily, which, however, did not cite a source. An autopsy confirmed that he had been cured of cancer, with no trace of the disease, and that he died three years after his recovery, though from a different diagnosis. EWTN News contacted Father Bogucki for details about the case and the alleged healing. Instead, the priest — who is of Polish origin, lived in Slovakia for many years, and served as a confessor at St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome — asked for prayers for the final phase before Sister Zdenka’s possible canonization. https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: BERLIN — Friedrich Merz’s center-left coalition partners increasingly see themselves facing a stark choice: Turn against the reform course they’ve struck with the chancellor or risk sinking with him. Following the conservatives’ stinging defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — a loss driven in great part by dissatisfaction with Merz and his party, the Christian Democratic Union — there are early signs the Social Democratic Party is turning against the series of reforms it has agreed to push through with the unpopular chancellor. The SPD’s pivot is likely to deepen Merz’s myriad challenges as questions mount over his ability to lead Germany’s relatively weak coalition government. Merz has acknowledged that his dismal approval ratings helped fuel the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, but argues that the answer is to press ahead with his reform agenda while doing a better job of explaining its necessity to voters. Advertisement Advertisement That’s not the conclusion his center-left coalition partners have drawn: They argue the problem isn’t one of messaging but of substance. “The path the federal government has taken with its reform plans has caused particular uncertainty,” Rasha Nasr, an SPD lawmaker in the Bundestag, told POLITICO’s Berlin Playbook Podcast . “It’s very important now that, unlike others in the coalition, we don’t just push this through. The people of Saxony-Anhalt have told us very clearly: ‘This far and no further,’” she added. Merz has staked his chancellorship on tackling economic and welfare reforms that previous governments deemed too politically difficult, even branding himself the “reform chancellor.” His agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth. SPD general secretary Tim Klüssendorf, who has said there are reform measures that need to be addressed, at a press conference after an SPD leadership meeting in Berlin in March 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images Until now, the SPD under the leadership of Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has advanced the reform drive, portraying itself as willing to undertake the tough choices needed to restore Germany’s economy while fighting inside the coalition to resist conservative excesses. But given Merz’s growing troubles — and rising questions about the durability of the coalition government — the party’s calculus appears to have changed. The shift also comes ahead of two additional state elections on Sept. 20 in which the SPD is hoping to score at least one much-needed win. Klingbeil signaled a course change already on the night of the Saxony-Anhalt election. The result provides “a reason to reflect on policies here in Berlin and on the federal government’s reform agenda,” Klingbeil told public broadcaster ZDF as votes were still being counted. “And rest assured, that’s exactly what we’ll do.” Advertisement Advertisement The open disagreement prompted the chancellor to discuss divisions between the coalition parties with SPD leaders Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas on Monday via phone, according to a senior government official who was granted anonymity to discuss internal matters. SPD hopes for redemption Given its own political weakness, the SPD is very unlikely to pull the plug on the current coalition — a move that would trigger new elections while its poll numbers are scraping historic lows. The party is currently polling at around 12 percent , 4.4 percentage points below its share of the vote in the 2025 federal election, which was its worst result in well over a century . But the recent signals from SPD leaders suggest they are looking ahead to their own political survival as Merz’s chancellorship grows increasingly precarious. Manuela Schwesig, the SPD premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania who has been able to cut into the AfD’s lead in the eastern state, campaigning in Luetzow on Aug. 21, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images It also comes as the SPD sees a rare glimmer of hope for an election boon that could restore some of the party’s battered political standing. In the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania ahead of a Sept. 20 election, the SPD’s incumbent premier, Manuela Schwesig, is polling a strong second behind the AfD. Under Schwesig — who ranks among Germany’s most well-liked politicians , according to surveys — the SPD has been able to cut into the far right’s lead in recent weeks. An SPD victory in the state — or even a serious challenge to the AfD’s lead — could give the beleaguered center-left party a desperately needed political boost. Advertisement Advertisement But what’s more significant for Germany’s coalition is the way Schwesig has at least in part attained her popularity: by railing against Merz’s reform drive, depicting the overhauls as harsh and unjust. “Yes, we need social reforms, the welfare state must be stabilized, and labor costs must not rise,” she told Welt TV on Monday. “But it is unacceptable that, of all people, those who work the hardest and contribute the most are the ones bearing the heaviest burden. Many people also perceive this as unfair. And that is why it is important to change course here.” Should the SPD congeal around Schwesig and her criticisms, it’s likely to further complicate Merz’s ability to govern and pass legislation that satisfies his increasingly restive conservative faction. ‘Unwavering determination’ Already, disagreements between the SPD and Merz’s conservatives are spilling into the open. SPD politicians are questioning the coalition’s previously agreed plan to make it harder for workers to take sick days, a measure that sparked public outrage and, for many, reinforced Merz’s image as lacking empathy with regular people. SPD politicians have also called for renewed state subsidies to lower fuel prices — a proposal Merz’s CDU rejects as too expensive. “Clearly, when it comes to specific measures, there are certainly issues we need to address this fall,” Tim Klüssendorf, the SPD’s general secretary, said of the reforms on German television this week. “Take, for example, pensions, long-term care, and health care, but also the question of whether we’re finally going to do something about these gas prices, including through regulatory measures. These are certainly the measures that must now be put on the table as a direct consequence of the election results.” Advertisement Advertisement Merz, for his part, is sticking to his line that people would agree to his reforms if they better understood their importance. “This is about nothing more and nothing less than the future of our country and the opportunities for our children and grandchildren,” he said Monday. “And we must not squander them. That is why my determination to continue on the path of reform remains unwavering.” Rasmus Buchsteiner contributed reporting.

ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT According to the drone unit of the 92nd Assault Brigade, the soldier was injured in a position where a conventional evacuation was impossible because of mines and Russian drone activity. The footage shows soldiers monitoring the operation from a control room as the wounded serviceman attaches himself to the drone and is lifted away from the danger zone. The drone is then seen carrying the soldier to a landing point, where he is brought safely back to the ground. Soldiers in the control room applaud after the operation. The brigade has not disclosed when or where the evacuation took place. https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/heal.text: OBITUARY Education People Miner’s son who rose to leading role in Scotland's largest council Education People By Herald Obituaries Share 0 Comments Ted Milburn (Image: Contributed) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Ted Milburn Born: July 10, 1938; Died: August 19, 2026 Professor Ted Milburn CBE has died after a life devoted to youth work and community education, rising to be assistant director of education in Strathclyde Region, at the time the largest local authority in Europe. Born in July 1938 in the market town of Morpeth, he was the only son of a nurse and a shop assistant. His father was George Milburn, who had been one of the miners locked out of the pits in 1926 by owners determined to have their workforce accept a 40% wage cut. George trained as a nurse in what was then known as an asylum, and contracted tuberculosis working with his patients during the blackout of the Second World War. Ted developed a primary form of the disease which meant he was absent for almost two years of primary education. His teacher recorded that he was “a nice boy, but he will never be a leader”, a judgement that meant he missed out on grammar school, attending a secondary modern instead. Ted started work as a clerk on the railway, but his early educational setback was no barrier to his career. He attended night classes in Newcastle and trained at the YMCA College in London and graduated with first class honours from the University of Sussex. He worked for the YMCA in Huddersfield and Brighton, ably supported by his first wife Joan. As head of the Marmion Centre in Brighton in the early 1960s, he saw beyond the moral panic surrounding the brawls between the Mods and Rockers, perceiving instead the individual needs of the young people concerned. He and his team opened the Marmion Centre to provide a service of hot food and shelter, reducing tension between the opposing groups. His early experiences led to a lifelong belief in second-chance learning, in creating environments where those who had been written off by early life experiences might thrive. A firm believer in seeing the potential in those who may have been held back by early disadvantage, he moved to Scotland in 1973 to become a community education officer in Renfrew Division, then to lecture at Strathclyde University, rising to be assistant director of education in Strathclyde Region. He returned to Strathclyde University as senior lecturer before being inaugurated as a professor of community education, the first in the UK. Read more Legend dead at 102: ‘blonde who has all the answers’ Eva Marie Saint | The Herald Jeffrey Archer: Monica Coghlan's life was destroyed by Archer's lies | The Herald Scottish singer Lena Martell dies as tributes paid | The Herald Ted’s affirmative approach to youth work was matched by his scholarly acumen and he was invited to write for a number of leading publishers in education. However, it was as a skilled communicator, a warm and supportive colleague, teacher and leader that he was best known. His services were in demand across the UK and Europe, including the Nordic countries but most particularly in the former soviet states of Moldova, Poland, Ukraine and Hungary. He was chair of the Princes Trust, president of the YMCA, director of the Centre for Youth Work Studies, editor of the Scottish Youth Issues Journal, and the inspiration for the Ted Milburn Scholarship, which awarded grants to students who would not otherwise be able to attend university. Ted was a genuinely humble man, welcoming any successes not as a personal accolade, but as an honour for the service of youth work and community education, an undervalued and often poorly funded arm of public service. He was an enabler, an encourager and a much-loved mentor. He was devoted to his students, many of whom went on to leading roles in education and local government. Ted is survived by his wife Jeannie and his children, Richard, Gordon and Lynda.
